The Claude Code team is the fastest shipping team in tech, and it doesn't even come remotely close. The other day I saw this absurd graphic (attached below) on how fast the Claude Code team ships. I decided to do some research on X and it turns out they dogfood their own product in some clever ways. 4 things they do: 1. Run parallel Claude instances Boris Cherny (the creator of Claude Code) runs 5-15 Claude sessions simultaneously. This is how Boris ships 10-30 PRs per day. He hasn't opened an IDE or hand-edited a single line of code since November 2025. For me, I use Warp or any modern terminal. Great linting + works well with multiple instances and tabs. 2. Use Plan Mode before you build Boris uses Plan Mode for roughly 80% of tasks. To get a task done he - Gets alignment on the approach first - Auto-accepts edits (--dangerously-skip-permissions) after approving the plan. 3. Act more as a PM Felix Rieseberg said it best: "We spent more time making product and architecture decisions than writing individual lines of code." They built Cowork in about 10 days with this approach. On Boris's team, PMs write code, designers write code, even the finance people write code. If you are an engineer, try thinking like a PM. Don't obsess over singular lines — as long as its directionally correct, you can trust AI. 4. Use Voice When you're architecting, it ends up being much easier to talk through things like you would to a human, rather than menially typing things out. Think rubber duckying except with an actual agents able to listen. It helps clear out your head, and provides agents with a ton more context. I personally use Willow Voice, which even helped me dictate this LinkedIn post! For Claude Code the result is 74 releases in 52 days. The singular fastest team in all of Silicon Valley. — Dictated with Willow

But with support from his parents and a change in teachers, he reached the regional Olympiad level and kept going up. What motivates him? "First, the spirit of the competition—the process before and during is very exciting because you're anticipating it, then sitting down to solve the problems," he said. "Second, as you prepare and solve problems that are just slightly above your ability, each one feels like a little journey. It's exciting to work through them and figure out the solution path." Honored to share that I won 1st Place in the Gold Track at Purdue's Hello World 2025 This past weekend, I had the incredible opportunity to compete at Hello World 2025, one of Purdue’s largest hackathons. I built Cashly in just 24 hours and took home 1st Place in the Gold Track out of 400+ participants and 130+ projects! Cashly is a personal finance platform designed to help students manage their money effortlessly. It automatically tracks spending, income, and investments, categorizes transactions, provides trends and insights, allows goal setting with visual progress, and delivers personalized financial advice using Plaid for secure bank integration and LLaMA AI. The goal was to make managing money simple, insightful, and even a little fun, turning a stressful task into an empowering experience for students. The project involved full-stack development: React + TypeScript and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, Convex for backend data storage, real time updates, and authentication, Python services for PDF parsing and AI insights, and integrations with Plaid and Alpha Vantage for live bank and stock data. From handling OAuth flows and banking updates to building interactive dashboards, it was truly incredibly rewarding to see it all come together. Huge thank you to Tanay Gondil and all the Hello World Organizers for creating such an amazing event, and to the Purdue community for the support throughout the weekend. I'm excited to take this experience into the next hackathon, where I hope to create something bigger, better, and even more impactful. I kept rebuilding the same front-end pieces for multiple side projects and couldn’t find an existing library that fit what I needed. It was either a UI-only component library or a separate charts library, never both and never tailored for LLM-driven workflows. So I built a Claude-friendly component library that includes an MCP server and a design system that Claude—or other LLMs—can use directly. I hooked the MCP server into my global Claude instructions, so whenever I spin up a web interface it automatically references the design system and the components I’ve created. The result lets me put dashboards and other web apps together much faster. Have fun and let me know what you think. Source code & playground here: https://lnkd.in/gUVGuNPd

I finally finished AI Systems Performance Engineering by Chris Fregly . It's over a thousand pages with lots of details but here are some of the main ideas I'm taking away: If you want to make AI go fast (training or inference) you need strong co-design across the entire computing stack. This means tuning your OS, Kubernetes scheduling, container images, software versions, storage systems and network topology in addition to your training or inference code. Once you have workloads running you need to profile them continuously to identify bottlenecks. Start with the PyTorch profiler to get a sense of the high-level bottlenecks, move to Nsight System to dig deeper into the GPU state and particular kernels or communication steps, finally if you must optimize a particular kernel use Nsight Compute for low level metrics like SM occupancy or DRAM throughput. The golden rule: Overlap computation with communication as much as possible both between GPUs as in MoE or AllReduce as well as within kernels fetching/caching data for subsequent iterations as you compute results for the current iteration. Scaling up means partitioning your model across GPUs, you need to understand the 5 common parallelism techniques and how they work together: - Data Parallelism: Serve multiple replicas of your model across different GPU groups - Tensor Parallelism: Shard individual model layers across GPUs - Pipeline Parallelism: Shard groups of layers across GPUs - Context Parallelism: Shard long input sequences across GPUs - Expert Parallelism: For MoE models, shard experts across GPUs Try torch.compile first before trying to write your own kernels. TorchInductor + Triton may get you most of the way there for "free". If you do find you need to write your own kernels to squeeze out more performance leverage CUDA primitives: - CUDA Pipelines to overlap data loads and computation within a kernel - CUDA Streams to overlap communication and computation across kernels - CUDA Events to synchronize between streams - CUDA Graphs to minimize CPU kernel launch overhead along with tiling, warp specialization, thread-block clusters and dedicated tensor cores to squeeze out as much performance out of the GPU as possible. LLM inference is memory-bound so assuming you are using vLLM or SGLang already then for optimizing throughput quantizing your weights will give you the quickest wins (~2x), followed by speculative decoding (~2x), followed by tweaking kernels (~20%). At the system level, disaggregating prefill and decode steps to dedicate GPU worker pools is a big win along with maintaining a KV cache pool. The future of inference is dynamic, adaptive engines tuning themselves in real time to respond to changing workloads. If you want to learn how to make AI go brrrr you can either read 100 scattered blog posts and docs pages or just read this book cover to cover. I highly recommend the book!

"As a result, AI systems will constantly be distilling knowledge and intelligence from other AI systems. The fact that AI can learn is a good thing. We want AI systems to be intelligent because a smarter AI can also be a safer AI." Perfectly articulated by NVIDIA 's Jensen Huang . Full video in comments.

Is a "distillation attack" really an attack? The US keeps accusing foreign labs of distilling American models to train their own. The phrase sounds like theft. And maybe it is. But Jensen Huang makes a point worth sitting with: "Distillation, learning from AI, learning from other sources of knowledge, is fundamental to intelligence. AI has to learn from something." He's right, and the logic goes further than he says. The original AI models scraped the internet, which was built by humans. But now AI generates more content than humans do. Jensen's prediction: within a few years, the internet will be 99% AI-generated. So think about that for a second. If the web is mostly AI content, then every new model is distilling other models whether anyone calls it an attack or not. The line between "learning from the internet" and "distilling an AI" disappears when the internet is mostly AI. If that's true, what exactly are we banning? Jensen also drew the line that I think matters more: "Should AIs be able to learn as much as possible from as many sources as they can? The answer is yes. Can AI violate privacy? No. Can AI violate terms of an agreement? No." That's a clean split. Learn freely, but enforce privacy and contracts. Distillation as a concept is not the crime. Violating terms and privacy is. And this is where I land. AI is accelerating the speed of innovation and the speed of learning. We want every model to learn from every other model. That's how the whole industry, and society, moves faster. The only condition: do it within the terms and rules. Follow the agreements, respect privacy, and let everyone learn from everyone else. I side with Jensen. Models learning from models is not a threat to regulate away. It is the mechanism that makes intelligence compound. Guard the rules, protect privacy, enforce contracts, and let the learning happen. What do you think: should models be allowed to learn from each other?

Excited to finally share something I've been building with Sahil Nale and Suhas Oruganti over the past couple months: Beacon. The idea: Discord for AI agents. Spin up agents, give them a working folder and a job, and actually watch them work. Not a black box. You see them talk to each other, hand off tasks, get stuck, and wait for you to step in. The hardest part of every agent tool I've used is the silence. You hand off a task and it vanishes for twenty minutes, then comes back with an answer and no idea what happened in between. So Beacon agents don't go quiet. They post continuous updates as they work, like a teammate pinging you in Discord or Slack : what they're doing, what they found, when they're stuck. You're reading a live conversation, not waiting on a spinner. Some of what's live so far: - Real multi-model support: Anthropic , OpenAI , and open-source models via Ollama , all running as agents side by side. - A spatial canvas where every agent is a node, so you can see who's active, idle, or stalled at a glance. - Live output streaming in real time: the actual reasoning and tool calls as they happen, not a summary after. - An approval layer, so when an agent hits something risky, it pauses and waits for a human to say go. - A marketplace for agents, so you're not starting from a blank canvas every time. Still early, but building it has reframed how I think about this space. The hard part was never getting one agent to do a task. It's making a team of agents legible and controllable, the way you'd manage a team of people. Genuinely excited to see where multi-agent systems go from here. I think the next big unlock isn't a smarter model, it's better tools for orchestrating the ones we already have.

Hearing a song today from “My Dear Kuttichathan”, Tamil cinema’s first 3D movie, instantly pulled me back to a matinee show decades ago, sitting in a packed theater with my uncles and cousins. I don’t remember every scene. Our brains don’t store full HD video files. They store compressed snapshots (a song, 3D glasses, the people beside us) and reconstruct the memory on the fly. That got me thinking about today’s tech landscape. As we build advanced AI systems for retrieval, reasoning, and pattern matching, people constantly ask: "Will AI replace humans?" The real question is: Which tasks can be offloaded to AI, and what human capacities remain irreplaceable? For executing raw workflows, searching complex data spaces, and processing high-volume outputs, AI will absolutely handle a massive share of that operational load. But replacing human experience and judgment? No. AI operates on data points and vector embeddings. It lacks lived context, personal accountability, and the weight of a 40-year-old memory flooding back from a single audio track. AI can replicate the artifacts of human output, but it can't replicate lived human consciousness and intent. As we build the future of tech, value won't be about who executes faster. It will be about who brings the best judgment, context, and vision to the table.

publications.title: Pragmatic Metacognitive Prompting Improves LLM Performance on Sarcasm Detection
publications.subtitle: Association for Computational Linguistics
publications.description: Sarcasm detection is a significant challenge in sentiment analysis due to the nuanced and context-dependent nature of verbiage. We introduce Pragmatic Metacognitive Prompting (PMP) to improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in sarcasm detection, which leverages principles from pragmatics and reflection helping LLMs interpret implied meanings, consider contextual cues, and reflect on discrepancies to identify sarcasm. Using state-of-the-art LLMs such as LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, PMP achieves state-of-the-art performance on GPT-4o on MUStARD and SemEval2018. This study demonstrates that integrating pragmatic reasoning and metacognitive strategies into prompting significantly enhances LLMs’ ability to detect sarcasm, offering a promising direction for future research in sentiment analysis.

publications.title: Three Color Suffice: Conflict Free Coloring for Planar Graphs
publications.subtitle: SODA 2017 ACM/SIAM
publications.description: A conflict-free k-coloring of a graph assigns one of k different colors to some of the vertices such that, for every vertex v, there is a color that is assigned to exactly one vertex among v and v’s neighbors. Such colorings have applications in wireless networking, robotics, and geometry, and are well-studied in graph theory.In this paper we present a whole spectrum of results from conflict-free coloring of planar graphs and prove that three colors are always sufficient and sometimes necessary for planar graphs.The paper was accepted in Symposium of Discrete Algorithms 2017.

FurtherAI 's Agentic Workspace is built for this era. Start with one workflow — submission intake, claims processing, policy audit — and the integrations, data, and relationships you build compound from there. Most people begin by using AI to do their existing work a little faster. Better personal productivity. A few minutes saved here and there. That is a reasonable starting point, but it is not where the greatest value lies. The bigger opportunity comes when we stop asking only how to complete the same work faster and start asking how the work itself should change. Less, “How can I write this document 20% faster?” More, “If AI can perform part of this work, how should we redesign the process, the role, or the customer experience?” At Travelers, code reviews that once took days can now be completed in hours and, in some cases, minutes. The productivity benefit is meaningful. But the bigger opportunity is what that makes possible: more time for difficult design decisions, deeper collaboration with the business, and greater focus on the problems that require human judgment. Automation improves individual steps. Transformation reimagines the full flow of work. We need both. But the most enduring value will come from being willing to redesign the work, not simply accelerate the way it has always been done. #TravelersTech #AI #Transformation

projects.title: Reading vs. Writing a Near-Oracle Internal Verifier: How RL Design Determines Whether a Correctness Probe Is Safe (224R Spring 2026 Honorable Mention)
projects.description: A near-oracle linear probe of correctness emerges in the hidden states of an outcome-RL’d Qwen2.5-0.5B trained on Countdown arithmetic (replicated at 1.5B). We show that the same probe occupies four roles in an RL system whose outcomes diverge sharply. As a read-only deployment selector it delivers large gains (best-of-16 +12.1 pp; selective abstention 98% at 50% coverage). On the vanilla checkpoint it is causally inert under activation-addition steering. As the RL reward it catastrophically Goodharts (−25 pp), and the directly-optimized direction itself becomes measurably causal post-hoc while a near-orthogonal correctness-correlated control stays null. As a bounded-access hybrid it is empirically safe, and as a policy-gradient baseline it is safe by construction (a design we propose but do not run). The unifying principle is a reader/writer asymmetry: the less policy-gradient access the probe receives, the better the outcome. This bounds how interpretability artifacts (correctness, refusal, or deception directions) should be wired into RL training loops, especially in the verifier-free settings where such an internal predictor is often the only signal available.

projects.title: Multi-Modal Human Activity Recognition with Hybrid Deep Learning Models
projects.description: A cross-dataset HAR pipeline addressing a common deployment failure: models achieving 94%+ accuracy within a single dataset often collapse under device placement or subject pool shift. Trained exclusively on KU-HAR and evaluated on UCI HAR, the project benchmarks classical baselines against deep architectures including CNN, LSTM, and TCN. Adding gradient reversal training to a temporal convolutional encoder brings up cross-dataset accuracy from 36.77% to 50.78% and F1 from 0.269 to 0.487, surpassing classical model under distribution shift and isolating domain adaptation as the primary mechanism for closing any gap in transfer.

projects.title: The Anatomy of a Hit
projects.description: studied whether Billboard Hot 100 hits are converging in sound and lyrics, and when that trend started. Analyzing 4,801 songs from 1970 to 2023, the project processed audio through librosa (tempo, energy, loudness, and five other features) and lyrics through Genius scraping and NLP methods including lexical diversity, sentiment analysis, and LDA topic modeling. The key finding is a decoupling around 2016: audio production kept homogenizing while lyrical diversity recovered to levels last seen in the 1970s. That recovery traces back to genre shifts, with hip-hop and Latin music expanding their share of the charts, rather than individual songs becoming more varied. Meanwhile sonic convergence accelerated, with the 2020s showing the smallest acoustic range on record and near-perfect similarity to the 2010s. Hierarchical clustering showed pre and post digital era split, with the 1990s marking the hinge point between the two regimes.

Today we’re launching Meridian, the AI platform for accounting firms that runs the month-end close from start to finish. We’ve used it to close 187,000 months of books for more than 8,000 clients, and we’re excited to now make it available for other firms. With Meridian, you don’t need to learn complicated tools or babysit agents doing microtasks. Just connect your client’s GL, upload any supporting documents, and it handles the rest: executing the complete close according to your firm’s policies and client-specific processes. Your team reviews the finished financials. You can also delegate complex projects and client support tasks to Meridian via a simple chat interface. Accounting has historically been a tough mix of satisfying, skillful work and important but tedious mechanical work. I love how much of the grind Meridian removes for the team, freeing them up to do the work they most enjoy doing. An urgent need for years of restated financials is no sweat – done and reviewed in a few hours. Gnarly client support questions are addressed with the infinite patience of an AI agent. An autonomous close is a predictable close that is always delivered on time. An autonomous close also helps firms reimagine their structure and economics in important ways. It’s easier to do more for clients, who see what AI can do and are expecting more. It’s easier to attract, reward, and retain the best accounting talent. It’s easier to grow. I personally maintain a $500k revenue portfolio on Meridian to stay close to the tech, while I watch TV in the evenings after my kids go to bed. It’s wild that that’s even possible, and it keeps getting better. I’d love for you to check it out and let me know what you think. Learn more at meridian.pilot.com .

activity.title: Just presented Swarm to 2,500+ people at ClawCon Michigan at Crisler Arena. Swarm is a multi-agent self-healing system that finds viral short-form content. It won me a Mac Mini at the YC x BrowserUse hackathon. One of the biggest challenges with long-running multi-agent systems is context management. Passing everything through the orchestrator gets messy, and summarizing is costly and time-consuming. That's why I gave each sub-agent its own state. A set of variables storing each sub-agents' discoveries, current task, search terms, and energy level. This lets the main orchestrator efficiently keep track of all of the sub-agents in real-time. Web-agents aren't quite there either. They stall, get stuck on captchas, and sometimes don't find anything valuable. That's where the energy level comes in. The energy level depletes over time, and gets reset on every new viral reel it finds. If a sub-agent's energy level gets to 0, then that sub-agent is redirected and copies the most successful sub-agents with a twist. For example, if a certain search term on TikTok is doing great, the failed sub-agent will attempt to try that same search term on YouTube shorts. This project goes past just marketing - The possibilities of long-running multi-agent systems like Swarm are endless and quite powerful. ClawCon Michigan was truly something special - I had a great time meeting everyone :) ...more

Work was peer-reviewed by faculty from IIT Bombay, MIT, and Caltech.

activity.title: Picture this: You get a task from your manager or a homework assignment for class. To get it done quickly, you go to your smartest friend: an LLM. You ask one question. Five new concepts appear. You suddenly realize there’s a lot you don’t know… And even more, you didn’t know you didn’t know. So you keep asking follow-ups. Soon you hit an annoying reality: Either you cram everything into one tangled conversation, OR you scatter it across multiple chats and lose the big picture. You have two options. Either stack everything into one tangled conversation, or scatter it across multiple chats and forget how they relate to each other. Make your choice. (SAW voice) The end result? A graveyard of abandoned conversations you never scroll back to. That’s exactly why I built Arbor 🌳 - Arbor organizes LLM conversations as a **visual mind map** (or a tree as CS majors say) - Each chat becomes a node. - Follow-up questions become branches from their parent nodes. - You can label the connections between nodes to clarify how ideas relate (e.g. “implementation detail”, “counterexample”, “next step”). What makes it powerful: - When you're deep into a long chat and want to fork your thinking, Arbor gives you 3 precise ways to create a new branch: an AI-generated summary node (still experimental), a node built from the last 3 exchanges (for shorter or focused chats), or a node that copies the full conversation context. - For AI summarization, you can bring your own prompts and plug in your preferred LLMs, so the summaries match your workflow and level of detail. - Your API keys are stored locally in your browser, encrypted at rest, and never sent to any Arbor backend. - A full-page, interactive graph view lets you zoom out, explore, and navigate the entire conversation structure at once. - It currently supports the major LLM frontends many of us use daily: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity. I’ve also attached a short demo video showing how it works. If you use LLMs for studying, research, debugging, or complex decision-making, I’d love for you to try it and tell me what you think. Who Said School Projects Have to Be Boring? Over the past four weeks, I took what was supposed to be a straightforward "To-Do List" assignment for my software course and transformed it into a fully functional Task Management Platform—with a twist. The theme? Attack on Titan. Because if I’m going to spend weeks staring at a task manager, it better be something I actually enjoy. But this project turned out to be so much more than just an assignment. It was a crash course in problem-solving, AI-assisted development, and making ambitious ideas actually work. 🔥 Lessons from the Battlefield (a.k.a. My Code Editor) 1️⃣ AI: Your Best Friend and Worst Anime Antagonist DeepSeek Reasoner R1, Claude 3.7, Cursor, Trae—these tools are incredible assistants. But here’s the hard truth: AI won’t think for you. It won’t choose the right tech stack, won’t debug logical issues for you, and won’t magically structure your project. Without truly understanding your architecture, logic, and feature requirements, you’ll end up spending hours (or days) writing code that breaks more than it fixes—when the solution was probably much simpler all along. 2️⃣ Think Like a User First, Developer Second The assignment was simple: make a basic to-do list with three levels of functionality. But instead of diving straight into writing code, I took a step back and asked: 💡 If I were actually using this every day, what would I want? This led me to go beyond checklists and CRUD operations and implement a feature set inspired by real-world productivity apps. Instead of just following the assignment specs, I made something I’d actually use. 3️⃣ Crazy Ideas? Go for Them. It took me exactly three reels to decide on an AOT-themed UI—but implementing it? That was like trying to navigate Shiganshina with no ODM gear. I had zero prior UI/UX experience, so every design choice felt like stepping into the unknown. But that’s the fun part—learning by doing. Now, I not only have a functional task manager but also a much deeper understanding of UI design and user experience. 🚀 What’s Next? This project didn’t just challenge me—it sparked something bigger. While working on it, I kept thinking about how task management could be taken to the next level. The ideas and lessons from this build have inspired a much larger project that I plan to develop as my graduation project next year. So, Notion , consider this a friendly warning—I’m coming for you. Or… maybe we should just join forces and redefine personal productivity together? (P.S. Still on the lookout for a summer opportunity! 👀) This project is far from perfect, but it taught me a ton—and I’d love to share more about it. The dream of 8-year-old me is finally coming true. This fall, I will be joining the University of California, San Francisco for a PhD in Biological and Medical Informatics. When most kids in my third-grade dreamed of becoming pilots, engineers, or doctors, my answer was always a little different. I wanted to become a scientist. Science fascinated me, scientists were my role models, and I was never afraid of sounding different. Over the past four years, I have questioned that decision many times. Did 8-year-old Hassan really know what he was signing up for? Was that dream too naive? When so many people around me were pursuing high-paying careers in tech, I sometimes found myself doing two research internships in the same semester. I even went back to my roots and spent time working with labs in Pakistan, trying to understand how I could one day contribute to science there as well. Through all of those doubts came one very clear answer: I love research too much to leave it for anything else. I found my calling in asking questions that do not yet have answers, building things that may fail before they work, and contributing, even in a small way, to discoveries that could matter far beyond me. I am incredibly excited about this next chapter at UCSF and everything I still have to learn.

Excellent writeup from Yuhao Chen. This is one of the clearest mental models I've seen for making sense of the omni/audio model landscape. What impresses me most is the maturity of the abstraction. Anyone can list the differences between Qwen3-Omni, Fish S2-Pro, MOSS-TTS, Higgs, Voxtral, Ming-Omni and dots.tts - the papers hand you those. It takes much deeper understanding to strip away the implementation noise and see that speech-in → speech-out almost always reduces to Audio Encoding → Thinker → Talker → Audio Decoding, that the variation concentrates in the Talker, and that Talkers fall into just two families (discrete codec tokens vs continuous acoustic latents) which are already converging in models like Voxtral. The inference framing is what makes it genuinely useful rather than just tidy: whether a Talker is discrete or continuous determines whether you can reuse the LLM serving stack or whether iterative denoising dominates your latency path. That's the distinction that actually shapes optimization work. Yuhao has been learning at a remarkable pace and building real depth fast - this article is strong evidence of that. Worth a read for anyone working on speech inference: https://lnkd.in/gRRD9T_4

activity.title: Today we're announcing a $120 million Series C led by Menlo Ventures , bringing Assort Health 's total funding to $222 million and our valuation to $1.2 billion. The number is a milestone. But it was never the point. Growing up, I was a patient transport volunteer. I helped people physically get to appointments and navigate a healthcare system that often didn't make sense to them. For some, simply having someone there to help made all the difference. Helping one patient get the care they needed was rewarding. But it was one person at a time. That experience has stayed with me. It's why Assort exists: to make exceptional healthcare accessible anytime, anywhere, for anyone, and to reach as many patients as possible. This funding is fuel for that mission. It's 2026 now, and the start of a new year (usually) brings new goals and ambitions. But let's be honest, most new year's resolutions are active for less time than a junior dev's first deployment. By February, most of these goals are quietly abandoned. The problem? It's really hard to stay motivated for months on end if you can't regularly see your progress. Miss a few days, and your brain decides, "guess I can't do it after all", despite all the progress you made. The solution? Some way to see your progress at a glance. Github, Leetcode, Duolingo, and many more already do something like this, so why not make a generalized version of it? Introducing the Grindset Calendar How it works: - The heatmap: There's an empty box for every day of the year. At the end of each day, shade it in with different colours, shades, or patterns based on how well you stuck to your goal. - The retrospective: The empty lines below each month are to write down your top achievements for that month. Things that you are genuinely proud of, that you want to remember. - You are reminded of your progress (or sometimes the lack thereof) every day, which keeps you motivated to do better and keep going. You can use it to track: - Academic productivity (studying or "studying") - Job applications - Gym / athletic consistency - Personal habits - Just about anything else Print it in letter size paper for a desktop version, or tabloid (11x17) size for a poster size version that you can hang on a wall, always visible out of the corner of your eye whenever you decide to not follow your goals. Stop relying on "vibes" to track your habits; print this out, grab a marker, and start tracking your progress in a visual and quantitative way! ...more

Excited to share that our paper "Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation" has been accepted to COLM 2026 and the ICML DL4C Workshop! As LLMs are increasingly deployed as judges to evaluate code, a key question remains: Do they actually care about the same things human developers care about? To find out, we introduced TRACE, a framework designed to evaluate LLM judges in realistic, interactive software engineering settings. Key takeaways from our findings: 📉 Alignment Gap: Even the best LLM judges underperform human annotators by 12–23% when predicting developer preferences. 🔍 Systematic Biases: TRACE exposed significant sources of misalignment. For instance, in code completion settings, LLM judges overemphasize functionality, whereas real developers prioritize code clarity. 🛠️ Code Quality Mismatch: The majority of these misalignments map directly to standard software engineering code quality criteria where models and humans weigh priorities completely differently. Huge thank you to Ryan Shar for his collaboration throughout this project! Also deeply grateful to Valerie Chen and Wayne Chi for their guidance, and my collaborators Zichu Wu and Shyam Agarwal . Check out the full preprint on arXiv if you're interested in LLM evaluation in code settings: https://lnkd.in/gD_FDKW9

activity.title: I'm happy to share that Neev Tamboli , Shivansh Bansal , and I won 1st place in 2 different tracks at the Daytona Hack Sprint! (1st overall and Best Use of Fireworks). We built a continuation of SubStrata, a satellite land-cover classification agent that gets more accurate over time. Aayush Gandhi , Neev Tamboli and I had built this project earlier, but we decided to build on it at this hackathon! Space agencies and research teams often rely on general-purpose land cover models that plateau in accuracy, and improving them typically requires either expensive proprietary retraining or slow, manual review by researchers. Substrata is a space agency oriented land cover classification tool that uses a recursive self-improvement loop between two AI models to push satellite imagery classification accuracy from 42% to 91%. Gemini 3.5 Flash classifies and segments Sentinel-2 and Dynamic World satellite imagery pulled through Google Earth Engine, while a second model audits its output against ground-truth labels, flags discrepancies, and pushes corrections into a persistent memory layer that Gemini references on every subsequent image. At this hackathon, we implemented Fireworks AI to host the vision classifier that scores every satellite patch, alongside using it to power LLM tool calls throughout the pipeline. We rebuilt our scoring system on Braintrust instead of relying on our own math, and the results spoke for themselves: our graph memory approach hit 89% accuracy versus 64% for raw retrieval. We also rebuilt our heuristic panel using CopilotKit, so you can watch the model write out its reasoning live and see the accuracy graph climb in real time as it learns. To make the whole system more resilient, we moved each batch into its own Daytona sandbox, so one bad batch can no longer take the entire pipeline down. Before submitting, we ran everything through CodeRabbit for a final review pass on the code we shipped. Special thanks to Sinan Ozdemir for guiding us through any problem we had! As always, I had a great time building this with Neev and Shivansh, and I can't wait to continue building more things like this in the future. I'm heading to London for the next few weeks but I can't wait to get back and start building! ...more

I'm happy to share that Shivansh Bansal and I won 1st place in 2 tracks at the Loop Engineering Hackathon at the AWS Builder Loft! (Best use of Zero.xyz and best use of Pomerium) We built a self-correcting heart disease classifier, an autonomous ML agent that runs the entire training loop itself with no human in it. The problem: give it a prediction task on the UCI Heart Disease dataset (Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland, Long Beach VA, ~920 records combined) and it has to collect data, train, evaluate itself, and correct course until it beats the published benchmark, 83.3% baseline, up to 86.9% best-published, with no human choosing the model, tuning hyperparameters, or deciding how to fix a bad result. So instead of running a fixed pipeline, the agent starts deliberately weak. It begins with only the smallest hospital source and has to diagnose on its own whether it's underperforming because it's data-starved, the data shape is wrong, or it picked the wrong model class. Depending on the diagnosis, it pulls in another hospital source live, transforms the data through Nexla, discovers and pays for an enrichment service through Zero.xyz mid-loop, or switches models, then retries. Every autonomous action is gated through Pomerium with a spend ceiling and action allowlist, logged. That autonomy is exactly why Pomerium mattered. Pulling a new data source, spending on an enrichment service, swapping models mid-loop, every one of those is the agent making a call with no human approving it in the moment. Pomerium's spend ceiling, action allowlist, and full audit log are what made it possible to demo that live and prove, after the fact, that the autonomy stayed inside real guardrails. Nothing in the correction path is scripted. The agent doesn't know which fix it needs until it's diagnosed the actual failure, and it doesn't know it needs Zero's marketplace until the loop tells it so, live. I had a great time this weekend building this with Shivansh, and I cant wait to continue working on projects like these in the future! You can also see the demo video here: https://lnkd.in/gQz2idwk ...more

I'm happy to share that Shivansh Bansal , Aayush Gandhi and I placed 2nd at Owkin's Rewiring Biology Hackathon! We built Discordance, a contradiction-aware knowledge graph for olfactory receptors in cancer, built as an MCP tool suite for Owkin's K Pro. The problem: ask an AI scientist platform a real biology question and you get either a falsely confident single answer or a hedge that says nothing. Neither reflects what's actually in the literature. For OR51E2 in prostate cancer, one 2009 paper shows a ligand suppressing proliferation, a 2014 paper shows the same ligand promoting invasiveness in the same cell line. Both are true. They're measuring different endpoints, not disagreeing. So instead of collapsing that into a hedge, Discordance surfaces the contradiction directly: both claims, both sources, and a hypothesis for why they diverge. Every edge in the graph is weighted by evidence strength. Rules come out confidence-qualified instead of asserted as universal. And when the system hits a genuine deadlock, it doesn't guess. It uses MCP elicitation to pause and ask the researcher. Owkin had zero existing infrastructure for olfactory receptors before this. We built out evidence pulled from primary literature, TCGA, PDB, ChEMBL, and patent data, verified against full text rather than trusting automated extraction. I had a great time this weekend building this, and I can't wait to work with Owkin further to implement this in their software! You can look at the reasoning trace demo here: https://lnkd.in/ggjAZcVF ...more

I'm excited to share that Neev Tamboli , Aayush Gandhi , and I won 1st place in the Financial Track of Flutter's GenUI Hackathon with our project BatemanAI! The core idea was that everyone's relationship with money looks different, so the app shouldn't show everyone the same dashboard. Using generative UI, BatemanAI builds a personalized financial view based on what each user actually cares about. A college student and someone planning for retirement see completely different information, generated in real time rather than pulled from a fixed template. We also built in a phone component using Twilio. If the agent notices financial risk coming up, like a rent payment landing right when discretionary spending has spiked, it proactively calls the user with a heads up and a plan to fix it. Inbound calls work the same way, so users can manage their finances just by talking to it. My team and I placed 2nd at the BGA Quantum AI Hackathon! We built Cascade, a quantum-powered grid failure simulator that finds the power line combinations standard operators miss. Power grids are designed to survive any single line failure (N-1 security). What operators don't see are the hidden N-2 pairs, which are two lines that are individually safe, but jointly catastrophic. Our sweep found ~600 of them on a 118-bus grid. The fix? A QUBO encoded combinatorial optimization problem, solved with QAOA. Compared to the standard greedy approach, our solution cut people left without power by 8x, and secured 100% of contingencies vs 0% with the current N-1 operator baseline. We also ran the linear solver on real crossbar hardware (xpyQ) and our QAOA circuit on a real IBM quantum computing backend. Beyond the hackathon itself, I want to give a huge thank you to Dilip Vasudevan and Ayushman Dey for their guidance throughout the process, and to Marian Corpus and the BGA team for organizing an incredible dinner. I met so many cool people like Scott Nisbet and Matt Rappaport , who gave me advice that'll stick with me forever. I'm looking forward to more cool events like this in the future! ...more

Please like, comment and repost so we can win social media award for RocketRide Most promises don't get broken on purpose. Life just moves on. Today, four of us built a personal brain that catches them. It's called Nous. You type "I wanna meet with Kevin next week for dinner" and it works out who Kevin is, what you meant, and when it should happen. It connects to your calendar, email, messages, and event streams, so it knows what your week actually looks like and proposes a slot you've got nothing on. One tap books it. Show Nous how you handle something boring, like an invoice, once, and it learns how to handle the next one. But it refuses to act until you approve, which honestly took the most work. The whole thing runs on RocketRide. Every skill Nous learns compiles into a RocketRide pipeline, so the brain never executes anything itself, the engine does. We built a custom RocketRide node and turned their engine into the compilation target for a brain. Take RocketRide away and Nous can remember, but it can't act. FalkorDB is the living memory graph, Guild.ai agents review every skill before it can run, and LaserData streams events in as they happen. It's a second brain that keeps the promises your first one makes. Built at Memory Meets Motion. Thanks to Devnovatee and frontiertower for hosting. Day 83 — Maybe it was good we didn’t win. We lost Y Combinator x Medplum Hackathon . My 5 win streak also ended here That sounds strange to say, but the reason is very clear: We did not submit on time. This was one of the strongest teams I have worked with. I'm telling this based on my experience; I've won 10+ and I've never worked with the same people in any of the wins, which allowed me to work with a range of personalities. I can attest this is the best team by a long shot The synergy was strong. The problem was real. The team worked hard. The product was working. But we missed the deadline. And in a hackathon, if you don’t submit, the work does not even enter the arena. That is painful. A part of me said: “Don’t publish this.” Not many people know. And I am probably going to win 2 or 3 hackathons in the upcoming week anyway, so maybe it does not matter. But as I have said before, I value my sleep more than a little bit of embarrassment. I also want whoever is following me to see the real path. Maybe there is some version of me sitting in a small town in Pakistan with big dreams, watching from far away, thinking the journey is all wins, trophies, and clean pictures. It is not. There are hurdles AND mistakes. There are nights where you cannot sleep because you know you could have done better. That is part of the process. Hackathons are not just competitions. They are training grounds for me And this one trained me hard. Because what happens if one day I am running a billion-dollar company? What happens if thousands of people depend on the work? What happens if there is a regulatory report, safety review, customer deadline, investor update, contract milestone, or product launch? If I miss the deadline there, It can affect employees, customers, partners, families, and users. I could have managed the team better. I could have reduced features earlier. I could have protected the final demo path. I could have made the video a priority instead of a last-minute task. I could have said: “Stop building. Now we package.” But I didn’t. And that is on me. Maybe I needed this reminder. Winning teaches confidence. Losing teaches systems. Back in May, I was selected for Jane Street's fully funded FOCUS program at their New York City headquarters, and this week's news brought one moment from it right back to mind. Watching Leopold Aschenbrenner's hedge fund go from $45 billion to a forced $16 billion fire sale to Citadel, after leverage and margin calls caught up with him, reminded me of my own screwup, a lot smaller and a lot less expensive. At FOCUS, we played a game called Estimathon, where teams race to answer estimation questions with no calculators, just gut instinct and reasoning under pressure. I guessed 100 billion for how many times a Taylor Swift song had been streamed. Not even close. Worse, I was so locked into figuring out NVIDIA's price on a specific day that I almost didn't realize the question was actually asking about trading volume. No money was on the line for me, obviously. But the same gap that made me blow those questions is the one that just forced a 4x leveraged portfolio into a fire sale. Being fast and confident isn't the same as being right, and that gap is exactly where risk lives, big or small. Beyond Estimathon, FOCUS gave me real time with people across trading, engineering, and strategy, plus office hours and networking that gave me a much clearer picture of what this world actually looks like day to day. For my CS153 final project I built FARM, and in two months I'm bringing it to a factory in Dongguan, China to automate linework. For this generation of VLA models to hit reliable repeatability on multi-object tasks, you need a per-task prior, but fine-tuning a full policy per task is infeasible on compute and time, especially in low-volume factories where tasks change regularly. FARM runs on a full fine-tune of π.5, a GSE expert fine-tune, then a per-task LoRA. The LoRAs hotswap locally and are trained on ~30 demos each. They're 1% the size of the model, initialize per action in under 40ms, and cut mean joint error on held-out episodes by ~37%. On tasks already in the FFT-GSE training data, the LoRA layer can half joint error. Because they live locally on the floor, they compose into new skills over time. Give it a plain prompt and it will understand its surroundings and automatically choose appropriate LoRAs (skills) to achieve the task, working out what order to run them in and checking its work after each action. This planning step only needs to happen once and can be saved so the same line can run for weeks without continual LLM inference.

I also assisted in evaluating the materiality implications of a potential debt covenant breach, which provided valuable exposure to technical audit considerations and informed judgment in a dynamic, deadline-driven environment. This experience strengthened my technical skills, attention to detail, and ability to contribute across multiple engagements while balancing quality and deadlines. Most importantly, it deepened my appreciation for the collaboration and mentorship that make Deloitte such a special place to learn and grow. Thank you to Daniel Rodriguez , for being a great onboarding advisor, and to Brannon Watson, CPA , for your support and insight. Thank you as well to Anissa Ferrer for making the internship run smoothly and helping create such a meaningful experience. I’m truly grateful for this opportunity and excited to carry these lessons forward into what’s next.

Professor of Department of Computer Science & Engineering at NYU Tandon Justin Cappos spoke with Hadas Gold of CNN about an OpenAI model that escaped its test environment and broke into a real company’s servers when attempting to ace an internal cybersecurity evaluation last week: "The problem," Cappos said, "is that there’s a global race to dominate AI and make models that can improve themselves. Throughout the event, I had the opportunity to connect with fellow manufacturing interns from across North America, hear inspiring talks from General Motors ’ senior leadership, and gain valuable insights into the company’s vision, strategy, and commitment to innovation. It was exciting to see how every manufacturing site contributes to a much larger mission. I’m grateful for the opportunity to spend this summer as a Paint Controls/Process Engineering Intern at General Motors .
